pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Determine whether a quantity (initially up to 20) is odd or even by pairing objects: even = every object has a partner (no leftover); odd = one left over. Even numbers can be written as two equal addends (8 = 4 + 4).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): counting in 2s and recognising odd/even patterns support number-structure work (KS1→Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.3 'determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g. by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends'.
• Operational details — Build odd/even from the concrete pairing action (line up objects in twos; is there a lone one?), link to skip-counting in 2s, and connect to the doubles fact (even = double of something). Later generalise the digit rule (look at the ones/last digit) but ground it first in the pairing structure so the rule is understood, not memorised.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): pairs objects to decide odd/even up to ~10. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): decides odd/even to 20 by pairing or counting in 2s and writes an even number as n + n. Tier C (age 8, extending): states and justifies the last-digit rule (0,2,4,6,8) and predicts odd/even for larger numbers.
bestPractices: Anchor in the pairing action first: arrange in twos and check for a leftover — the definition, not a memorised list.
Link to counting in 2s and to doubles (even numbers are doubles), connecting three ideas.
Have children write even numbers as equal addends (8 = 4 + 4) to formalise 'made of pairs'.
Introduce the last-digit shortcut only AFTER the pairing meaning is secure, and justify it via the pairs in the ones.
Use two-column / ten-frame arrangements so 'paired vs one sticking out' is visually obvious.
keyRepresentations: Objects arranged in two rows / pairs (leftover = odd)
Ten-frame (pairs in columns; a lone counter shows odd)
Number track coloured by odd/even (alternating pattern)
Counting-in-2s hops on a number line
Doubles facts (n + n) linked to even numbers
commonMisconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about being 'big/small' or arbitrary, not about pairing.
Confusing odd/even with the count of digits or with multiples of other numbers.
Believing 0 is odd, or being unsure whether 0/2 are even.
Memorising the last-digit rule with no grasp of why (can't justify).
Miscounting pairs and so misclassifying near-boundary numbers.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: build the meaning of odd/even from the pairing action — line up objects two-by-two and check for a leftover (even = everything pairs, odd = one left over). Ground the concept in pairing, counting in 2s, and doubles (even = n + n) before introducing the last-digit shortcut, so the rule is understood rather than memorised.

activities.title: Pair-them-up frame
feedback: If the learner thinks odd/even depends on the number being big or small, show a small odd number and a large even number side by side so size is decoupled from parity.
When a counter is stranded, highlight it (e.g. it glows or wobbles alone) and name it 'the leftover with no partner — that's what odd means'.
When the slider ticks up, prompt: 'Did adding one make a new pair, or leave one stranded? What does that make the number now?'
When a child writes 8 = 4 + 4, connect it to the frame: 'four pairs, or two equal groups of four — that's why it's even.'
activities.rationale: Odd/even is defined by the pairing action, so letting the child change the count and watch the parity flip makes the alternating structure and the doubles link concrete. The live recolouring, lone-counter highlight, slider, and equal-addends strip are optional interaction examples that make the pairing mechanism visible; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s, and write an even number as a sum of two equal addends (2.OA.3).
Odd/even should be grounded in the pairing structure and doubles before the last-digit rule is introduced.
learnerActions: Choose a number of counters (start up to 10, then up to 20) and drop them into a two-row frame so they arrange into pairs.
Look at the result: if one counter is left with no partner the number is ODD; if every counter is matched the number is EVEN.
Use a slider or counter to add one and remove one, watching whether the lone counter appears or disappears each time.
Say out loud what changes each step: adding one either strands a single counter (makes it odd) or creates a new pair (makes it even).
Use an 'equal addends' strip to write each even number as n + n (e.g. 8 = 4 + 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A number is even when its objects pair with none left over and odd when exactly one is left over; because adding one either completes a pair or strands a single, odd and even alternate, and every even number is a double (n + n).

activities.title: Predict then check with real counters
feedback: If a child says 13 is even because 'you can split it into 7 and 6', have them line the 7 and 6 up in pairs and show that one is stranded — even means pairs with none left over, so the two groups must be equal.
If a child answers instantly from size ('even because it's big'), show small and large numbers of each parity so size is clearly not the rule.
If the reasoning is right ('one left over means odd') but the count slips, slow the one-to-one matching and recount the leftover pile — the concept is intact; support the counting.
For 0: there is nothing left unpaired, so 0 is even — invite the child to articulate this with the 'none left over' definition.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a stated reason exposes whether a child treats 'odd' as an unpairable leftover or just as a label, and separates conceptual misunderstanding (unequal-split or size rules) from simple miscounting.
sourceClaims: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s, and write an even number as a sum of two equal addends (2.OA.3).
learnerActions: Take a pile of counters (e.g. 13). Before touching them, predict whether they will all get a partner or whether one will be left over, and say why.
Pair them two-by-two to check your prediction.
Discuss: why is 13 odd but 12 even — what changes when you add one more?
Tackle a friend's claim that 'zero is odd because there's nothing to pair', and decide whether 0 is odd or even.
Try reasoning about a large number (e.g. 100 or 24 or 47): how could you tell odd or even without pairing every one?
activities.intendedInsight: Parity is about whether everything pairs with nothing left over, not about size or whether the number can be split into any two groups; this reasoning generalises to larger numbers.

activities.title: Counting in 2s and the last-digit rule
feedback: If a child recites the last-digit rule but cannot justify it, pair up a ten to show it makes 5 pairs with none left over, then return to pairing in the ones and ask why those digits leave no leftover.
If skip-counting and pairing give different answers, recount together — both methods should agree for the same number.
Link each even result back to a double (n + n) to reinforce that even numbers are made of pairs.
activities.rationale: The last-digit shortcut is introduced only after the pairing meaning is built, so it is understood and justifiable rather than memorised; counting in 2s and the coloured number track connect three representations of the same idea. This activity targets the extending tier (Tier C) where children justify the rule and predict for larger numbers.
sourceClaims: Odd/even should be grounded in the pairing structure and doubles before the last-digit rule is introduced.
Counting in 2s and recognising odd/even number patterns are part of the primary number curriculum.
learnerActions: Count a group by 2s (hop along a number line in twos) to decide if the total is even, and compare this with the pairing result for the same number.
Colour a number track by odd and even to reveal the alternating pattern.
After the pairing meaning is secure, look at the ones digit of several numbers (e.g. 20, 12, 24, 16, 18, 47, 53) and notice which digits (0,2,4,6,8) go with even.

State and justify the last-digit rule by reasoning that every ten makes 5 pairs with none left over, so whether there is a leftover depends only on the ones; then use it to predict the parity of a larger number.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in 2s, the alternating number-track pattern, and the last-digit rule all describe the same pairing structure; the digit shortcut is a justified consequence of pairing, not a memorised fact.

constraints: Anchor the concept in the pairing action first; introduce the last-digit shortcut only after the pairing meaning is secure and have children justify it: every ten splits into 5 pairs with none left over, so only the ones can leave a leftover.
'Even' means pairs with none left over — equal pairing. Splitting a number into any two groups (e.g. 13 as 7 and 6) does not make it even; the groups must be equal.
0 is even (nothing is left unpaired); address the 'zero is odd' claim explicitly rather than leaving it ambiguous.
Decouple parity from size: deliberately show small odd numbers and large even numbers so children do not infer parity from magnitude.

A sorting/categorising or multiple-choice task (sort into odd/even bins, fill 8 = __ + __, choose and explain) is suitable for consolidation once the pairing meaning is built; such a task can check or reinforce classification but does not by itself elicit the independent pairing construction and explanation.

A static paired-vs-leftover illustration with tap-to-reveal is a useful reference, but it cannot be manipulated by the child; the alternation insight is stronger when the learner changes the count and watches the parity flip.
Use two-column / ten-frame arrangements so 'paired vs one sticking out' is visually obvious; these can be physical counters or an on-screen model.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS 2.OA.3 and the NCETM pairing-before-rule claim) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Do not treat the unverified claims as confirmed.

The source material frames open dialogue and 3D manipulatives as 'poor' fits for this concept. Those are catalog fit rankings, not evidence of universal inefficacy — discussion is used productively here in the predict-then-check and zero-is-even reasoning, and the planar nature of pairing is a specific reason 3D adds little for this particular task, not a universal law.

Self-audit: pairing/parity logic checked — adding one to an even number strands a single (odd); adding one to an odd number completes a pair (even); alternation holds. 0 is even. 8 = 4 + 4 is correct. Ones digits of 20/24 are even, 47/53 are odd. The 'split into 7 and 6' example is correctly flagged as a misconception (unequal groups), not taught as valid.
The source misconception 'confusing odd/even with the count of digits or with multiples of other numbers' is only implicitly addressed; a dedicated probe could be added if desired.

assess.poeTask: Give the child 13 counters. Before touching them, ask: 'If you pair these two-by-two, will they all get a partner, or will one be left over?' Have them commit to a prediction and say why, THEN pair to check. The pre-observation reason exposes whether 'odd' is understood as an unpairable leftover or just a label.
probeDeeper: Why is 13 odd but 12 even — what changes when you add one more?
What if it had been 100 counters — how could you tell odd or even without pairing every one?
A friend says 'zero is odd because there's nothing to pair.' What would you say?
Show me with these counters what 'one left over' looks like.
assess.correctAnswer: Odd — if you pair the 13 up (two by two), there is one left over that has no partner; a number is even only when everything pairs with nothing left over.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's even because you can make two groups — 7 and 6.' Treats 'can be split into two groups' as the definition of even, ignoring that the groups must be equal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with counters: make the two groups, then line them up in pairs — show 7 and 6 do not match and one is stranded. Define even as 'pairs with none left over'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Even — you can split it into a group of 7 and a group of 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls 13 (or 7, 9) even and justifies with any two-way split rather than pairing into twos.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges odd/even by how big the number is or whether it 'looks like' a counting-by-twos number, e.g. thinks large numbers are even.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ground the judgement in the ones digit and in pairing; show small and large numbers of each parity so size is decoupled from parity.
errorPatterns.distractor: Even — thirteen is a biggish number so it's even.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers instantly from the size of 13 with no pairing reasoning, or says 'even because it's big'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Has the pairing idea but miscounts the counters and reports the wrong leftover, e.g. pairs 12 and forgets the 13th.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the count — slow the one-to-one, recount the leftover pile — do not reteach the odd/even concept, which is intact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasoning is correct ('one left over means odd') but the count of counters or of leftovers slips.

responseLevels.gap: Answers from size or an unequal-split rule; calls 13 even, or gives 'odd' with no pairing reason.
responseLevels.full: States odd because pairing leaves one over, generalises to 'even = pairs with none left / ends in 0,2,4,6,8', and predicts parity of a new number (e.g. 24, 47) by rule.
responseLevels.partial: Says odd and can pair counters to show the leftover for 13, but cannot yet state the general rule or predict a new number without laying it out.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 13 odd or even? How do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the pairing/grouping idea says 'odd, because one is left over'. A child who only knows a size rule or a 'split into two groups' rule will accept 13 as even (7 and 6 are two groups) or guess from magnitude, so the REASON — not the answer alone — separates them.
